messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kenneth had always taken pride in his work. For twenty-six years, he drove the same route through the northern suburbs, knowing every pothole, every stoplight, every regular face that climbed aboard with a nod or a quick “Morning, Ken.” The bus was his domain—a predictable, controlled space. That was before the night shift three years ago, when he gave a lift to a man he vaguely recognized from the depot. The man asked for a ride to the far end of the line, and Kenneth, tired from a double shift, agreed. He didn't think twice until the man moved into the seat behind him, until the engine idled at the empty terminus, until the unexpected hand on his shoulder. By the time it was over, Kenneth's world had shrunk to the smell of diesel and the sound of his own shallow breathing. He never reported it. He never told anyone. He just drove home, showered, and lay awake until dawn, certain that if he said the word out loud, the shame would swallow him whole.

In the months that followed, Kenneth discovered that the memory would not stay buried. It played like a film he could not switch off—the rough fabric of the seat, the weight, the low murmur of the man's voice, and worst of all, the terror that rushed back each time, as fresh as the moment itself. He began to notice that certain things pulled the film to the surface without warning. The sound of a bus door hissing shut could do it. A passenger clearing his throat in a particular pitch. And the exhaustion: when he was tired, the images seemed to break through the dam, flooding his mind until his hands trembled on the steering wheel. He learned to dread the late-afternoon runs, when fatigue crept into his bones and the film started to roll.

Driving with people became unbearable. Every passenger was a potential threat. He watched them in the rearview mirror—studying their hands, their posture, the direction of their gaze. He had come to believe that strangers were not simply unpredictable but dangerous; that any one of them could decide to cross a line. The bus, once his sanctuary, now felt like a trap. He started taking unscheduled breaks, pulling over to calm his racing heart. He switched to the earliest morning shift to minimize contact with rowdy riders, but the isolation cost him. His wife, Diane, noticed he was distant, that he flinched when she touched his shoulder from behind. He told her he was just stressed from work. He could not bring himself to explain the shame that clung to his body—the sense that he was dirty, damaged, that if anyone knew what had happened, they would see it written on his skin.

The lost faith was the quietest wound. Kenneth had never been particularly religious, but he had believed in a basic decency, a kind of unspoken contract between people. That contract was broken. He no longer trusted the goodwill of others, and in darker moments he saw the entire world as a place where someone could smile at you and then hurt you. He stopped attending the monthly drivers' social. He stopped greeting passengers with more than a grunt. When a young man offered him a coffee at a layover, Kenneth declined with a curt shake of his head, his jaw tight.

It was a sound that finally drove him to seek help. A few weeks ago, sitting in his idling bus at a red light, he heard a muffled thump from the luggage compartment—a passenger's bag shifting. The sound echoed something from the assault, a dull impact he had tried to forget. He lurched forward, slammed the brakes, and a woman in the front seat stumbled and nearly fell. She yelled at him, called him reckless. Kenneth pulled over, handed the wheel to a supervisor, and walked home. That night, Diane told him he needed to talk to someone. She said she was scared for him. She said she didn't know who he was anymore.

At fifty-three, Kenneth sits in the therapist's office with his hands clenched on his knees. He is afraid of what he might find if he opens the door to that memory—afraid that the shame will be too heavy, that the terror will never stop, that he will lose the last shreds of control he has left. But he is also tired, so tired, of living inside a film that never ends. He wants to get behind the wheel again without watching every face. He wants to look at Diane and feel her touch without flinching. He does not know if that is possible, but for the first time, he is willing to try.
